tagline: An Army post, a river town and a gold camp’s foundations
intro: The Fort Churchill to Wellington Back Country Byway runs 67 miles between its namesake places. The Bureau of Land Management classifies it as a Type I and Type II backcountry drive and recommends four to five hours for the journey. Its description emphasizes Fort Churchill’s history, while noting that some stretches may require a high-clearance vehicle.

The fort began after the Pyramid Lake War, when Captain Joseph Stewart established a permanent Army post along the Carson River. Construction started in July 1860 and finished in 1861; the post guarded settlers and Pony Express mail and became a Union Army supply depot. The Army abandoned it in 1869. Samuel Buckland later salvaged material from the dismantled buildings for a two-story replacement at his nearby way station. The fort entered Nevada’s state park system in 1957. A later park addition protected a Carson River corridor linking the old military site with Lahontan State Recreation Area.

Begin at Fort Churchill’s preserved ruins beside the Carson River. Dayton brings another Carson River setting, where water supported ore milling; Como’s gold-camp history belongs to the Pine Nut Mountains. The journey ends at Wellington, a town on State Route 208 named for a stagecoach businessman.

moments.title: Fort Churchill
moments.text: Fort Churchill’s ruins preserve the outline of a post that outlived its military purpose by becoming a historic site. During the Civil War, the fort served as a Union supply depot with an average strength of 200 soldiers. After its abandonment in 1869, the buildings sold at auction for $750 when Nevada declined to take them. Preservation came later: the ruins were partially restored to arrested decay with National Park Service help, and the Civilian Conservation Corps built the visitor center. Signs along the self-guided trail explain the individual buildings.

moments.title: Dayton
moments.text: The Carson River helped make Dayton a milling town. Travelers stopping for water at this bend once chose between following the river south and continuing west, giving the place its early name, Ponderers Rest. Gold mining brought settlement, and river water later supported the Comstock’s first major milling center. The Virginia and Truckee Railroad’s opening in 1869 shifted ore processing upstream to Carson River Canyon. The town’s economy changed again when a courthouse fire preceded the transfer of the county seat to Yerington in 1911. The local museum occupies an 1865 schoolhouse in the historic part of town.

moments.title: Como
moments.text: Foundations are what remain of Como’s buildings, but an 1863 visitor described a town with four hotels, eight saloons and a brewery. The correspondent, writing for the Sonoma County Democrat, visited in February, shortly after Como’s establishment during the Palmyra district’s gold rush in late 1862. That December, Nevada’s territorial legislature approved a charter for a toll road from Como to the Carson River and a bridge across it. Its newspaper, the Como Sentinel, ran from April to July 1864; the publishers then moved on to a newspaper in Dayton. The abandoned town now retains foundations and abandoned mines.
